𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀.

The debate is no longer limited to government employment and public education. A growing question is whether reservation should also extend to 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲-𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.

The constitutional framework primarily rests on 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝟭𝟰, 𝟭𝟱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝟭𝟲. 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝟭𝟱(𝟰) enables special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs, while Article 16(4) permits reservation in public employment for inadequately represented backward classes.

Article 15(5) already extends reservation to private unaided educational institutions, subject to the protection available to minority institutions under Article 30. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment introduced EWS reservation through Articles 15(6) and 16(6), which was upheld in 𝗝𝗮𝗻𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗔𝗯𝗵𝗶𝘆𝗮𝗻 𝘃. 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮 (𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟮).

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲-𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗲, however, raises difficult constitutional questions.

Supporters argue that the shrinking public sector limits the practical reach of reservation and that discrimination in private hiring continues. Opponents point to Article 19(1)(g), economic efficiency, business autonomy and the absence of an express constitutional mandate for reservation in private employment.

The issue becomes even more significant after *𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗣𝘂𝗻𝗷𝗮𝗯 𝘃. 𝗗𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗵 (𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟰)*, where the Supreme Court recognised the constitutional permissibility of SC/ST sub-classification.

Ultimately, reservation must balance 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲, 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆, 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗼𝗺.

The Constitution’s challenge is not merely to provide representation, but to create genuine equality of opportunity.

comment: A key practical issue is implementation: private-sector reservation would need clear criteria and oversight mechanisms to prevent token compliance while ensuring genuine inclusion without undermining merit and competitiveness.
